before.content_html:
A Site Made of Water

Your specified site for 2027 is not a building. The Spanish Armada campaign of 1588 is examined as a historic environment: the Channel and its winds, the ports on each shore, an exposed anchorage at Calais, the sandbanks off the Dutch coast, and the storm-lashed route home around Scotland and Ireland. The 16-mark question will ask how far a study of the Armada supports some statement, and the marks sit exactly where this lesson looks: in how geography shaped the outcome. Lesson 8 covers why Philip launched the Armada; this lesson follows the fleet through the environment that destroyed it.

The Plan and Its Geographical Flaw

Philip’s plan — the Enterprise of England — was not for the Armada to invade on its own. Its 130 ships carried perhaps eighteen thousand soldiers, but the real invasion army was the Duke of Parma’s veteran force in the Spanish Netherlands. The Armada’s job was to sweep up the Channel, join Parma, and escort his troops across the narrow sea in barges. The flaw was on the map from the start: Spain held no deep-water port anywhere along the invasion coast. Parma’s embarkation ports at Dunkirk and Nieuwpoort were shallow, fringed by sandbanks, and watched by Dutch flyboats that could sail where galleons could not. The Armada therefore had nowhere safe to wait, and the rendezvous depended on a fleet and an army, hundreds of miles apart with no fast communication, arriving in the same place at the same moment.

Key Fact

There was no deep-water port in friendly hands between Spain and Parma’s army. The Armada could reach the Netherlands coast — but it could not wait there safely, and Parma’s shallow ports were blockaded by Dutch flyboats his escorts could not clear.

Two Fleets Built for Different Battles

The commander Philip appointed after his best admiral died, the Duke of Medina Sidonia, led a fleet built around big, high-sided ships packed with soldiers, designed to grapple and board — to turn a sea fight into a land fight on wet decks. The English fleet, under Lord Howard of Effingham with Francis Drake as his deputy, was built on the opposite theory: race-built galleons, faster and more weatherly, carrying long-range culverins, crewed by sailors rather than soldiers. Just as important was where each fleet slept: the English operated from their own ports — Plymouth, then the anchorages up-Channel — with powder, shot, food and repairs a day away. Every mile the Armada sailed took it further from any harbour that could help it.

Up the Channel: The Crescent and the Weather Gauge

The Armada was sighted off the Lizard on 19 July 1588, and warning beacons carried the news along the coast faster than any rider. For a week the two fleets ran east up the Channel, and the fighting settled into a pattern set by wind and formation. Medina Sidonia sailed in a disciplined crescent, his strongest warships at the tips, transports sheltered inside — a formation the English could harass but not break. The English, holding the weather gauge, attacked from windward at Plymouth, Portland Bill and the Isle of Wight, staying at culverin range and refusing to close where Spanish soldiers could board. A week of running battle cost the Armada only a few ships — but it reached Calais with ammunition low, no port to enter, and Parma not ready.

Chains of hilltop beacons ran along the south coast and inland to London — pitch-soaked fires on high ground, each visible from the next. Lit in sequence, they could carry the alarm across southern England in hours. The system is a site feature worth naming: it meant the English fleet and the militia mustering at Tilbury reacted to the Armada’s movements at a speed Philip’s planners, working on months-old information, could not match.

Calais: An Anchorage That Doomed the Fleet

On 27 July the Armada anchored off Calais — not a harbour, just an open roadstead, exposed to wind and enemy alike, because there was nowhere else to go. Parma sent word he needed almost a week more, and his barges could not move while the flyboats prowled the banks. The English needed no week. On the night of 28 July they sent eight fireships, stuffed with pitch and gunpowder with guns left loaded to fire as they burned, down the wind into the anchorage. Against ships at anchor in the dark, packed close, the threat was terror itself. The Spanish captains cut their anchor cables to escape — and the crescent, which gunfire had never broken, ceased to exist in a single night. The cut cables would collect their price later: a fleet without anchors cannot hold itself off a storm coast.

Key Fact

Escaping the fireships, the Spanish captains cut their cables and abandoned their best anchors on the seabed off Calais. Weeks later, on the storm coasts of Scotland and Ireland, ships that could not anchor were driven ashore — a one-night decision at the site with a months-long consequence.

Gravelines and the Wind That Changed Twice

Off Gravelines on 29 July the English finally fought the battle they wanted: close enough for their guns to hurt, far enough to refuse boarding, against a scattered enemy short of shot. Several Spanish ships were sunk or driven ashore and many more were battered. Then the environment nearly finished the campaign at a stroke: the wind pushed the fleet towards the Zeeland sandbanks, shoaling water with no sea room, and only a shift of wind at the last moment let the Armada claw off into the North Sea. The same shift settled the campaign’s direction — with the English behind them and the wind foul for the Channel, the only way home was north-about, around Scotland and Ireland.

The Long Way Home

The route home killed more ships than the English had. Autumn gales caught a battered fleet on some of the most dangerous coasts in Europe; ships without anchors, with storm-damaged hulls and starving crews, were wrecked in numbers on the Scottish isles and above all on the west coast of Ireland. Perhaps half the fleet never reached Spain, and thousands of men died of drowning, disease and starvation — far more than died to English gunfire. Victory did not spare the victors either: typhus and dysentery swept the English fleet in the weeks after Gravelines, and sailors who had saved the kingdom died unpaid in the ports they had defended. Elizabeth’s famous appearance before the army at Tilbury came while the Armada was already limping north — the image of victory, minted as the environment completed it.

Using the Campaign as Your Site

Work in chains of feature and consequence. The missing deep-water port explains why the Armada was at anchor in an open roadstead at Calais; the roadstead explains why fireships worked; the cut cables explain the wrecks on the Irish coast; the sandbanks off Zeeland explain why Gravelines nearly ended everything; the home ports and beacon chains explain English speed and stamina; the north-about route explains why a fleet that lost few ships in battle lost half its strength getting home. Whatever the statement in the question, tie each claim to a named feature of this seaborne site and its consequence.

practice_questions.text: ‘The anchorage at Calais was the main reason the Armada failed.’ How far does a study of the Armada campaign support this statement? Explain your answer. You should refer to the campaign and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
Support for the statement (site evidence):
• Calais was an open roadstead, not a harbour: the fleet lay exposed to wind and to attack, with no shelter, no repairs and no resupply.
• Ships anchored close together in the open were the perfect target for fireships; the crescent that a week of gunfire had failed to break was scattered in a single night.
• Cutting the cables to escape left the fleet without its best anchors, which is why so many ships were driven ashore on the Scottish and Irish coasts weeks later.
Against the statement (site evidence and context):
• The fleet was only at Calais because Spain held no deep-water port on the invasion coast — the flaw was on the map before the anchorage was ever used.
• Parma’s army could not come out while Dutch flyboats watched the shallow ports of Dunkirk and Nieuwpoort, so the rendezvous would have failed anyway.
• Race-built galleons, culverins and English home ports won the running fight up the Channel and the close action at Gravelines on 29 July.
• Autumn storms on the north-about route home destroyed more ships than any single moment of the campaign.

[16 marks, with 4 further marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar — reach a judgement on the statement using the site and your contextual knowledge.]

Mastering: Site features linked to wider events, both sides weighed, sustained judgement.
Secure: Site features used with relevant contextual knowledge and a judgement.
Developing: Some site detail with limited wider context.
Emerging: Simple description of the site.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the English fleet’s ships and home ports in 1588.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Race-built galleons — longer, lower and faster than the Spanish ships, designed for gunnery rather than boarding.
• Long-range culverins, allowing the English to bombard from distances at which Spanish soldiers could not grapple and board.
• Home ports along the Channel (Plymouth and the anchorages up-Channel), giving resupply of powder, shot and food that the Armada, far from any friendly harbour, could not match.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about Spain’s lack of a deep-water port for the outcome of the Armada campaign.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It broke the rendezvous: the Armada could not wait safely anywhere near Parma's army, while Dunkirk and Nieuwpoort were too shallow for the galleons and blockaded by Dutch flyboats.
• It forced the fleet into the exposed Calais roadstead — the precondition for the fireship attack that broke the crescent without a battle.
• It denied repair and resupply: every English ship fought a day's sail from a friendly port; the Armada fought at the end of a supply line stretching to Spain.
• Ultimately it made the whole plan depend on perfect timing between a fleet and an army that could not communicate — a flaw visible on the map before a shot was fired.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how the fireship attack at Calais changed the course of the Armada campaign.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The situation on 27 July: the Armada anchored in the open roadstead, ammunition low, Parma needing days he did not have, the English fleet anchored to windward.
• The attack: eight fireships, loaded with pitch and powder, sent down the wind in darkness into the packed anchorage.
• The immediate result: captains cut their cables; the crescent formation that a week of gunnery had failed to break was scattered in one night.
• The consequences: the scattered fleet was caught at Gravelines short of shot; the abandoned anchors doomed ships on the storm coasts of the north-about route home.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the weather in the defeat of the Spanish Armada.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The weather gauge: holding the upwind position let the English choose the range and timing of every engagement in the Channel.
• The double shift after Gravelines: wind first drove the Armada towards the Zeeland sandbanks, then backed just in time to spare it — but pushed it into the North Sea, making the north-about route the only way home.
• The autumn gales: storms on the Scottish and Irish coasts destroyed more ships than English gunfire, finishing a fleet that could no longer anchor.
• Balance: weather alone does not explain the defeat — the plan's geographical flaw and English gunnery created the situation the storms completed; 'God blew and they were scattered' was propaganda as well as piety.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: 'The Spanish Armada was defeated by geography rather than by the English navy.' How far does a study of the Armada campaign support this statement? Explain your answer. You should refer to the campaign and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
Support for the statement (site evidence):
• The missing deep-water port made the rendezvous with Parma close to impossible before the fleets ever met.
• The Calais roadstead's exposure enabled the fireships; the Zeeland banks nearly wrecked the fleet; the north-about route and Atlantic storms destroyed perhaps half of it — far more than battle did.
Against the statement (site evidence and context):
• English choices exploited the geography: refusing to board, holding the weather gauge, striking with fireships at the one moment the anchorage made them decisive.
• Race-built ships and culverins won Gravelines on gunnery, breaking ships and morale before the storms took over.
• The Dutch flyboat blockade — allied action, not geography — pinned Parma in port.
A developed judgement weighing environmental causes against human agency is required for the top level.

before.content_html:
A Castle Rebuilt Around One Guest

Kenilworth Castle is your specified site for the 2028 exam. It is a medieval fortress in Warwickshire — Norman keep, great mere, John of Gaunt’s hall — but the exam is not really about the Middle Ages. It is about what Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester, did to the place in the 1570s, and above all about nineteen days in July 1575 when he staged the most lavish entertainment of the reign for Elizabeth I. Read the site properly and it opens up half your course: the court, royal progresses, the marriage question, and the politics of spending money to be loved.

Dudley and the Gift of a Castle

Kenilworth came to Dudley from the queen herself: she granted him the castle in 1563, the year before she made him Earl of Leicester. He was her favourite — the man she called her ‘eyes’, master of the horse, privy councillor, and for decades the most plausible husband she never took (Lesson 3). The gift was typical of how Elizabeth ruled her court: favour made visible in land and stone. What Dudley then spent on the place turned a royal gift into a royal argument — a castle rebuilt as a machine for entertaining one woman.

Key Fact

Elizabeth granted Kenilworth to Robert Dudley in 1563. For her visits he added a four-storey tower of state apartments — Leicester’s Building — raised a grand new gatehouse, modernised the medieval keep with great windows, and laid out a privy garden fit for a queen.

Reading the Site: What Leicester Built

The additions are still legible in the ruins, and each one is evidence. Leicester’s Building was a slender four-storey block of glittering state apartments, built so the queen and her ladies could lodge in modern comfort beside the medieval great hall — a private palace bolted onto a fortress. The gatehouse gave arriving courtiers a fashionable first impression (and survives intact, because later owners made it a house). The Norman keep was kept — twelfth-century mass declaring the antiquity of the place — but Leicester punched huge windows into it, dressing ancient strength in Elizabethan glass. And below the walls he laid out the privy garden: terraces, obelisks, an aviary of exotic birds, a marble fountain — recorded in such detail by an eyewitness that English Heritage rebuilt it in 2009. Around it all lay the mere, the vast lake that had made medieval Kenilworth almost siege-proof and that Leicester turned into a stage.

Notice what he did not build: nothing military. Kenilworth in the 1570s shows old defences repurposed as display — but here the purpose was sharper than status. Every stone was aimed at the queen’s opinion.

The Nineteen Days of 1575

Elizabeth had visited before — 1566, 1568, 1572 — but the visit of 9 to 27 July 1575 outdid everything in the reign: the longest stay she made at any courtier’s house. Leicester met her with a floating ‘Lady of the Lake’ welcoming her to a castle of legend; fireworks were reportedly heard twenty miles away; there was hunting by day and masques by night, bear-baiting, an Italian tumbler, and a swimming pageant in the mere where a performer as Arion, the legendary musician of Greek myth, rode a mechanical dolphin. Contemporaries claimed the entertainment cost Leicester a fortune — a figure of a thousand pounds a day was bandied about, though historians think what Leicester actually spent was a good deal lower than the gossip claimed. We know the detail because two eyewitness accounts survive: a long gossipy letter attributed to Robert Langham, a minor court official, and the poet George Gascoigne’s Princely Pleasures.

Most historians read 1575 as Leicester’s last grand bid for Elizabeth’s hand. The pageants said it almost openly — masques of marriage and of a lady released from an enchanted lake — and one planned entertainment pressing the theme was, tellingly, never performed; historians suspect the queen declined to hear it. She was forty-one, and hopes of the Leicester match were fading; and she left Kenilworth unmarried, as she left everywhere. For your exam, the visit is the marriage question (Lesson 3) staged in fireworks — and refused.

What the Site Shows About Elizabethan England

Kenilworth in 1575 is the court system working at full power. It shows how progresses let Elizabeth be seen by her people and fed at her courtiers’ expense — power displayed while someone else paid. It shows what favour was worth: a castle, offices and income flowed to Dudley, and he poured them back into loyalty spectacular enough for the whole kingdom to hear about. It shows the marriage question as living politics, played out in allegory before thousands. And it shows the propaganda machinery of the reign — poets, pageants and print carrying the event far beyond Warwickshire. The gossip, expense and spectacle of those nineteen days are as much a primary source for Elizabeth’s rule as any statute.

Key Fact

Two eyewitness accounts preserve the 1575 visit: the letter attributed to Robert Langham describing the festivities and the garden, and George Gascoigne’s Princely Pleasures at Kenilworth. Detail from the Langham letter guided English Heritage’s 2009 reconstruction of the Elizabethan garden.

The Site Afterwards and in the Exam

Leicester died in 1588, deep in debt. The castle passed on, was slighted after the Civil War in 1650 — the keep’s north side blown out, the mere drained — and settled into ruin. Today English Heritage keeps the shell, the gatehouse, the rebuilt garden and the empty basin of the mere. In the 16-mark question, chain features to meanings: Leicester’s Building → the cost of hosting the queen; the garden and pageants → courtship politics; the mere as stage → medieval strength repurposed as theatre; the gift of 1563 → how favour worked. Then weigh the site against your contextual knowledge of the court, progresses and the marriage question.

practice_questions.text: ‘Leicester rebuilt Kenilworth to win the queen, not to display his own greatness.’ How far does a study of Kenilworth support this statement? Explain your answer. You should refer to Kenilworth and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
Support for the statement (site evidence):
• Leicester’s Building was a four-storey block of state apartments raised so the queen and her ladies could be lodged in modern comfort beside the medieval hall.
• The privy garden below the walls — terraces, obelisks, aviary and fountain — was laid out for royal eyes, and was rebuilt by English Heritage from an eyewitness description.
• The 1575 entertainments argued in allegory for the queen’s hand, and one entertainment pressing the theme was never performed.
Against the statement (site evidence and context):
• The new gatehouse and the great windows cut into the Norman keep advertised Leicester’s own wealth and taste to every visitor, whether or not the queen came.
• Kenilworth was a royal gift of 1563; keeping it magnificent protected his standing at court and showed what favour was worth.
• A progress served purposes beyond courtship — royal visibility, hospitality to the whole travelling court, and the display of an orderly realm.

[16 marks, with 4 further marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar — reach a judgement on the statement using the site and your contextual knowledge.]

Mastering: Site features linked to wider events, both sides weighed, sustained judgement.
Secure: Site features used with relevant contextual knowledge and a judgement.
Developing: Some site detail with limited wider context.
Emerging: Simple description of the site.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the entertainments staged at Kenilworth in July 1575.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The Lady of the Lake pageant welcoming Elizabeth across the mere on her arrival.
• A swimming pageant with a performer as Arion riding a mechanical dolphin on the lake.
• Fireworks reportedly heard many miles away, masques by night and hunting by day.
• The sheer duration and cost — nineteen days, with gossip claiming a thousand pounds a day.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about royal progresses for Elizabeth’s style of rule, using Kenilworth as your example.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Visibility: progresses displayed the queen to her subjects across the country — monarchy performed in person, with Kenilworth 1575 its most spectacular stage.
• Economy: courtiers bore the crushing cost of hosting, so the crown bought magnificence with favour instead of money.
• Control of the elite: the hope and expense of a visit kept nobles competing to demonstrate loyalty — Leicester rebuilt a castle for the privilege.
• Propaganda reach: printed accounts like Gascoigne's carried the spectacle far beyond those present.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of Elizabeth's visit to Kenilworth in July 1575.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Arrival, 9 July: greeted by pageantry including the Lady of the Lake welcoming her to the castle across the mere.
• The stay: nineteen days of hunting, bear-baiting, masques, fireworks heard at great distance, and the Arion water pageant on the lake.
• The subtext: entertainments of courtship and marriage, with one pressing entertainment never performed — read by most historians as Leicester's final bid for her hand.
• Departure, 27 July: the queen left unmarried; the visit passed into legend through the Langham letter and Gascoigne's Princely Pleasures.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about what the 1575 visit cost Leicester.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It measures what royal favour was worth pursuing: contemporaries spoke of a thousand pounds a day, on top of years of building — spending aimed at one listener.
• It shows the court economy: Elizabeth's gift of the castle in 1563 flowed back to her as hospitality — favour converted to loyalty and display.
• It shows the risk side of the system: Leicester died in 1588 heavily in debt; competitive magnificence could ruin even the greatest favourite.
• It strengthens the courtship reading: expenditure this extreme fits a suit for the queen's hand, not routine hospitality.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: 'Kenilworth in 1575 shows that entertainment was really politics at Elizabeth's court.' How far does a study of Kenilworth support this statement? Explain your answer. You should refer to Kenilworth and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
Support for the statement (site evidence):
• The pageants argued in allegory — the Lady of the Lake and marriage masques staged Leicester's suit; the unperformed entertainment suggests a message the queen declined to hear.
• The buildings themselves were political instruments: Leicester's Building and the garden existed to honour and persuade one guest.
• The scale of spending only makes sense as investment in favour — the currency of Elizabethan politics.
Against the statement (site evidence and context):
• Much of the programme was straightforward pleasure — hunting, fireworks, acrobats — the shared culture of the court rather than coded argument.
• The politics had limits: the spectacular suit failed; Elizabeth kept the marriage question unanswered here as everywhere, suggesting entertainment could ask but never decide.
• Progresses served purposes beyond courtship — royal visibility and the display of a loyal, orderly realm.
A developed judgement on how far pleasure and politics can be separated at this court is required for the top level.
